messages.subject: Removing Axis Numbers
messages.body_plain:
A few days ago I posted asking how to NOT plot numbers below the x-axis.

I received many answers for which I am grateful and also a few requests to
post the solution:

To not plot values below the x-axis (or to plot values other than
standard) use the "scales" command within the "xyplot" function:

scales=list(x=list(at=0,labels=""))

within the xyplot makes the plot with no values on the x-axis.

xyplot(conc~log(diam,2),xlab='Size (um)', ylab=list('Concentration
(counts/mL)'), scales=list(x=list(at=log(c(1,3,5,10,15,20,30),2),
labels=c(" 1"," 3"," 5","10","15","20","30"))))

would plot 1, 3, 5, etc. at values of log(1), log(3), etc.

Scales takes a list so you can also do the same for the y-axis.

Many thanks to all who responded!

Jason

messages.subject: Re: t-test for binary data
messages.body_plain:
At 05:12 2/11/00 +0800, Xao Ping wrote:
>Dear All:
>I have two samples of different lengths containing binary varaibles (1,0).
>I need to figure out whether or not the probabilities of success  are 
>significally different in this samples. Which test should I apply?
>Thank you
>Xao Ping
>R&R Farmakinetics
>Taiwan

In fact if you just go ahead and do an ordinary t-test as if the data were
normally distributed you probably won't get a very different result from
what you would get if you did the more conventional thing and used a
chi-squared test.  Here is an example:

> s1 <- rbinom(20, 1, 0.6)
> s1
 [1] 1 1 0 1 0 0 1 0 1 0 1 0 1 0 0 0 0 1 1 1
> s2 <- rbinom(30, 1, 0.5)
> t.test(s1, s2)

        Standard Two-Sample t-Test

data:  s1 and s2 
t = -0.6871, df = 48, p-value = 0.4953 
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means is not equal to 0 
95 percent confidence interval:
 -0.39262  0.19262 
sample estimates:
 mean of x mean of y 
       0.5       0.6

---

OK, now here is the more conventional way of going about things using a
chi-squared test:

---

> m <- rbind(table(s1), table(s2))
> m
      0  1 
[1,] 10 10
[2,] 12 18
> chisq.test(m)

        Pearson's chi-square test with Yates' continuity correction

data:  m 
X-square = 0.1657, df = 1, p-value = 0.6839 

---

That looks pretty different, but most of this is due to Yates' correction:

---

> chisq.test(m, correct = F)

        Pearson's chi-square test without Yates' continuity correction

data:  m 
X-square = 0.487, df = 1, p-value = 0.4853 

---

The p-value is very close to that for the t-test and even the statistics
are numerically very close if you square the t-statistic:

> (-0.6871)^2
[1] 0.47211

In fact apart from the rather finnicky Yates' correction the differences
are (a) the t-test uses a pooled estimate of variance whereas the
chi-squared test lumps both samples together and (b) the t-test uses a
t-value for the cutoff whereas the chi-squared test uses a squared normal
value.

I mention this because I find most people never notice the connexion and
get very uptight about using normal theory approximations for cases where
the assumed normal distribution for observations is patently nonsense.
Care IS needed, of course, but in many respects the assumption of normality
is often not critical, (at least in univariate case).  What is usually much
more important is the assumption of low third and fourth cumulants, i.e.
reasonable symmetry and no huge outliers.

Here endeth the lesson for today...  :-)

Well, not quite.  Notice that I say "chi-squareD" test, not "chi-square"
test.  I'm finnicky that way, too!

Bill Venables.
--

messages.subject: Interface issues
messages.body_plain:
Thanks to the many people who replied to my inquiry about managing the
command window and scripts.  Here is a summary of the replies.  To save
time, I will not identify the individuals who provided each suggestion, but
thanks to all.

1) Several people reminded me to post my version and OS when posting.
(Windows NT, S+ 2000)
2) Use the script window instead of the command window.  Scripts can then be
saved and recalled.
3) Open the history window for better access to commands, easier cutting and
posting, etc.
4) Save the history window, and recall it at startup by setting a system
environment variable:  S_CMDFILE=+history.ssc
5) Use a REXX script (let me know if you would like the example mailed to
me) or separate icons to start sessions with different data directories
specified on the command line, as described in the manual.
6) Use EMACS and ESS for the interface. [Does anyone know a location with
good directions on getting this installed under Windoze?]
7) In the command window, set the prompt to whitespace using old <-
options(prompt=" ").
8) Write a function to switch between data directories.  This poster sent an
example, let me know if you would like a copy.  The note also suggested that
there may be fairly extensive suites of functions written for this purpose.

Eric Turkheimer
University of Virginia

messages.subject: Likelihood as a class.
messages.body_plain:
Has anyone tried defining likelihood as a class in S-Plus? A likelihood
object would be a function over a parameter space. Methods would extract
properties such a likelihood intervals.

Functions would allow one to eliminate nuisance parameters by different
techniques such as profiling, leading to a new likelihood object.

The interest is to develop a series of methods etc to implement
likelihood based inference along the lines in Royall's book "Statistical
evidence: A likelihood paradigm".

Rather than re-invent wheels and make the same mistakes that others have
done before, I thought I would ask if anyone has been down this road
already. I expect one of you clever chaps has thought this through
already.

James Roger.

Thanks a lot to Gérald Jean, James L. Pratt, Matthew Zack, Dave Atkins,
Andrzej Galecki, Patrick Connolly, Chuck Cleland, Nick Ellis and
Zhaorong Jiao. And thanks to this great list ! The original question is
given at the bottom of this message.

ANSWER:
The .L, .Q, and .C suffixes stand for linear, quadratic, and cubic
coefficients for an ordered polynomial. It was suggested in several
answers that contrast treatment "contr.treatment" may be more readily
interpretable than polynomial contrasts. This can be change with the
command:

options(contrasts=c(factor='contr.treatment',ordered='contr.treatment'))

following reference:

S. D. Walter;A. R. Feinstein;C. K. Wells 19??. Coding ordinal
independent variables in multiple regression analyses. American J. of

messages.subject: YAGS (GEE solver) revisions
messages.body_plain:
YAGS (Yet Another GEE Solver) version 2.x (see below for
value of x) is now available for testing.  A ~625K shar
file of Splus and C++ sources is available at
 
http://www.biostat.harvard.edu/~carey/ydown.html
 
Prof. Brian Ripley has graciously prepared a port for
Windows S-PLUS 4.x/2000 at
 
http://www.stats.ox.ac.uk/pub/SWin/yags2.zip
 
and this will be mirrored at statlib.  Until the
statlib mirror is updated, I will provide a copy
of the windows version at ydown.html mentioned
above.
 
Major modification: the main fitting function now presents a
"hardcode" option.  When selected, the GEE is solved in
a C++-coded shared object, providing solutions much more
rapidly for independence, exchangeable, AR(1) and unstructured
working correlation models.  The flexibility (and slow
performance) of pure Splus yags is not affected by revision.
C++ sources and compilation directives are supplied, but
some experience with finding necessary C++/g++ libraries
may be required to get satisfactory installation of the
C++ engine.  The code has been tested in Splus 5.1 and 3.4
under SunOS 5.5 and 5.6, and under both Splus5 and Splus6
(beta) under RedHat 6.1.
 
Additional information is at the ydown URL noted above.
An html document is included in the distribution.

E-mail comments to the address below.

VJ Carey

messages.subject: Configuring S-Plus for removeable media
messages.body_plain:
We've pretty much settled on purchasing an academic site license for 
S-Plus.  We've got a bunch of Windoze labs running either NT Server (with 
NT clients) or Windows 2000 Server with NT clients.  The Info Tech people 
do not want students saving information to the hard drives or the 
server.  Hence students are expected to supply either Zip disks or 1.44 MB 
floppies and keep *all* their information on it.  This means that their 
data, their preferences, etc must always be loaded from removeable 
media.  They can never be guaranteed the same machine or the same lab ever.

What is the most efficient way for students to (1) preserve the user, 
_Data, and _Prefs directory in this situation and (2) to execute/restore 
same to *any* networked computer that has the S-Plus executables, 
libraries, help files, etc on it.

My own experience has always been in a single user environment, and S-Plus 
is not very intuitive or user-friendly when it comes to creating different 
project directories in that setting either.

Thanks to input from Jorge Sirgo <jorge.sirgo at us.pwcglobal.com>
and others I have updated sas.get for S-Plus users who have
already installed the Hmisc library, to allow importing SAS
version 8 data into S-Plus.  sas.get imports SAS PROC FORMAT
value labels into S-Plus factor levels, imports variable
labels in "label" attributes, handles special missing values,
and other things.  It will support SAS variable names of
any length.  The new version may be downloaded from
hesweb1.med.virginia.edu/biostat/s/sas.get.s until it
makes its way into Hmisc (which I will announce in the future).

a .Data or _Data area (preferably ...library/Hmisc/_Data or
...library/Hmisc/.Data).  In S-Plus 2000 you can open the
file in a script window and submit it for loading into
S-Plus.  If you don't install the new sas.get over the
existing one in Hmisc/... be sure to delete the function when
you next re-load the whole Hmisc library.

sas.get runs on S-Plus 4.x and 2000 for Windoze, and 3.x for UNIX.
It may also work on S-Plus 3.x for Windoze.  In about 2 weeks all of
the Hmisc library will be available for S-Plus 6.0 on 
Intel Linux, followed by S-Plus 6.0 for UNIX.  The new version
of Hmisc may also work with S-Plus 5.1 but no guarantees.
Hmisc for S-Plus 4.x, 2000, and 3.x will be updated in about

messages.subject: Parameters in rweibull
messages.body_plain:
Hi, all, 

Please check out the following bizarre results about rweibull.

> N <- 1e5; alpha <- 2; lambda <- 10
> t <- rweibull(N, shape=alpha, scale=lambda)
# Sample Mean  vs. True Mean
> c(mean(t), gamma(1+1/alpha) / lambda^(1/alpha) )
[1] 8.8457266 0.2802496

Surprisingly, when and almost only when lambda is fixed at 1, these
numbers match each other very well. But when lambda is away from 1, there
always exists a big difference between the sample mean and the true mean.
Here I am following notations in Klein & Moeschberger (1997)'s survival
analysis book. And the survival functon of a weibull r.v. can be written
as   S(x) = \exp (-\lambda x^\alpha).

Is there something wrong with my understanding of the parametrization? 

Thanks a lot in advance for the help. 

Xiaogang Su

One Shields Avenue               E-mail: xgsu at wald.ucdavis.edu

messages.subject: Re: Parameters in rweibull
messages.body_plain:
On Fri, 3 Nov 2000, Xiao Gang Su wrote:

> 
> Hi, all, 
> 
> Please check out the following bizarre results about rweibull.
> 
> > N <- 1e5; alpha <- 2; lambda <- 10
> > t <- rweibull(N, shape=alpha, scale=lambda)
> # Sample Mean  vs. True Mean
> > c(mean(t), gamma(1+1/alpha) / lambda^(1/alpha) )
> [1] 8.8457266 0.2802496
> 
> Surprisingly, when and almost only when lambda is fixed at 1, these
> numbers match each other very well. But when lambda is away from 1, there
> always exists a big difference between the sample mean and the true mean.
> Here I am following notations in Klein & Moeschberger (1997)'s survival
> analysis book. And the survival functon of a weibull r.v. can be written
> as   S(x) = \exp (-\lambda x^\alpha).
> 
> Is there something wrong with my understanding of the parametrization? 

Yes.  Scale is not lambda. lambda is scale^{-alpha}. The survival
function used by S is

S(x) = \exp (-(x/scale)^\alpha).

so the mean is proportional to scale.

> t <- rweibull(N, shape=alpha, scale=10^(-0.5))
> c(mean(t), gamma(1+1/alpha) / lambda^(1/alpha) )
[1] 0.2813343 0.2802496

--

Call for papers
===============
  IDA-2001 will take place in Lisbon from  13th to 15th September 2001,  and
is organised by the Department of Computer Science of the Faculty of Science
and  Technology  of the  New  University  of Lisbon.  It will  consist  of a
stimulating  program  of tutorials,  invited talks  by leading international
experts in intelligent  data  analysis, contributed papers, poster sessions,
and an exciting social program.
  Our aim is for IDA-2001 to bring  together a wide  variety of  researchers
concerned  with  extracting  knowledge  from  data,  including  people  from
statistics,  machine learning,  neural networks,  computer science,  pattern
recognition, database management, and other areas. The strategies adopted by
people from these areas are  often different,  and a synergy results if this
is recognised. IDA-2001 is intended  to stimulate interaction  between these
different areas, so that more powerful tools emerge for extracting knowledge
from  data  and  a  better  understanding  is  developed  of the  process of
intelligent data analysis.

It is the fourth symposium on Intelligent Data Analysis after the successful

            factor2=levels(factor2),covariable=constant)
to make a data frame and hand that data frame to predict( ).
This approach is especially useful when there are interactions;
it makes one conscious of the levels of interacting factors.

Sometimes we need differences in predicted values and confidence
limits for those.  You can use predict to output the design matrix,
take the appropriate differences in its rows, and use the covariance
matrix formula for a linear combination of betas.  In the Design
library this is made easier with the contrast function, e.g.
contrast(fit, list(treatment='a', animal='dog'), 
              list(treatment='b', animal='cat'))
which will contrast a dog on treat a with a cat on treat b (not
that this is the usual contrast of interest).  -Frank Harrell

Hi,
I have an example when the z-value and p-value from a coxph output do not
agree. The difference is very small but exists.

I wonder if anyone encountered this problem: 

> fit
Call:
coxph(formula = Surv(ltime, lcens) ~ stg4 + stg3, data = npc)

      coef exp(coef) se(coef)     z     p 
stg4 0.855      2.35    0.479 1.784 0.074
stg3 0.473      1.61    0.581 0.814 0.420

Likelihood ratio test=3.56  on 2 df, p=0.169  n= 92 

BUT: 
 > 2*(1-pnorm(0.814))
[1] 0.415645

This p-value is different than one listed by the original output.

Also if I calculate z-value based on the coefficients and the variance I
get:

[1,] 0.2296711 0.1675666

coef_fit$coefficients

So the z-value fits with the original output but not the p-value.

> 
> BUT:

> [1] 0.415645

Only by rounding the output.  The code in S-PLUS 3.4 and 5.1 is 

                tmp <- cbind(coef, exp(coef), se, coef/se, signif(1 -
pchisq((coef/se)^2, 1), digits - 1))

What value do you have options(digits) set at?  If you have 7, 
digits is 3 and so you have 2 significant figures.

I really think this arbitrary manipulation of precision in the survival
routines is crazy, but after ten years' of complaining have given up on
it.

messages.subject: naive question re imputation and prediction
messages.subject_clean: naive question re imputation and prediction
messages.body_plain:
This is not specifically an S+ question.  Apologies if I am off topic.

I have a dataset that looks a bit like Swiss cheese, for which I am trying 
to produce a good prediction equation.  Imputation seems the obvious way to 
fill in some of the holes.  When I impute the missing values several 
variables are significant in regressions, whereas they are not when missing 
data are simply deleted.  These results are useful in helping me infer 
relationships among variables.  Yet for some reason I am not entirely 
comfortable building a prediction equation using data with imputed 
values.  I would prefer instead to build a predictive model based on a 
smaller subset of data with no missing values, accept the slightly larger 
error, and acknowledge that other variables may have explanatory power when 
there are more complete data.  That is, I am more comfortable using 
imputation for description than for prediction.  Is there any justification 
to my discomfort?

I am a non-statistician and would appreciate it if anyone could point me to 
a primer that addresses this specific topic (i.e., prediction with imputed 
values versus exploratory analysis).

Many thanks,

Todd Hatfield

> This is not specifically an S+ question.  Apologies if I am off topic.

> I have a dataset that looks a bit like Swiss cheese, for which I am trying
> to produce a good prediction equation.  Imputation seems the obvious way to
> fill in some of the holes.  When I impute the missing values several
> variables are significant in regressions, whereas they are not when missing
> data are simply deleted.  These results are useful in helping me infer
> relationships among variables.  Yet for some reason I am not entirely
> comfortable building a prediction equation using data with imputed
> values.  I would prefer instead to build a predictive model based on a
> smaller subset of data with no missing values, accept the slightly larger
> error, and acknowledge that other variables may have explanatory power when
> there are more complete data.  That is, I am more comfortable using
> imputation for description than for prediction.  Is there any justification
> to my discomfort?

No, afraid not.  One thing that is routinely worse than imputation is
casewise deletion.  Do make sure that you did multiple imputation, which
can use Y to predict missing Xs.  If you do this with single conditional
mean imputation, you can inflate relationships.

If you haven't seen it already, take a look at the Hmisc library's
transcan and fit.mult.impute functions:
http://hesweb1.med.virginia.edu/biostat/s/help/transcan.html

There are some nice web resources on imputation.  See links at
http://hesweb1.med.virginia.edu/biostat/rms

-Frank Harrell

messages.body_plain:
Hi, S+ users, provided below is a summary of responses I got for the Box
plot questions. I got so many answers from so many wonderful people. Tony
Lee, Jim Pratt and Jason Corner  suggested  making groups for columns of
data. Daniel Erdwin and Sally Rodriguez divided a graph sheet using "mfrow"
command. Laura Chihara and Greg Snow explained how to rearrange columns in
drop down menu for a Box plot. Naomi Robbins used an Excel work sheet to
concatenate several column data to a single column and  group the column
data in another column. Robert Garret provided Splus help files. Greg Snow
suggested creating another 3 column data/ rearranging data in drop down

        -----Original Message-----
        From:   Prof Brian D Ripley [SMTP:ripley at stats.ox.ac.uk]
        Sent:   Monday, November 06, 2000 3:49 PM
        To:     Pintilie, Melania
        Cc:     'S news'
        Subject:        Re: [S] p-value in coxph

        On Mon, 6 Nov 2000, Pintilie, Melania wrote:

        > Hi,
        > I have an example when the z-value and p-value from a coxph output
do not
        > agree. The difference is very small but exists.
        > 
        > I wonder if anyone encountered this problem: 
        > 
        > > fit
        > Call:
        > coxph(formula = Surv(ltime, lcens) ~ stg4 + stg3, data = npc)
        > 
        > 
        >       coef exp(coef) se(coef)     z     p 
        > stg4 0.855      2.35    0.479 1.784 0.074
        > stg3 0.473      1.61    0.581 0.814 0.420
        > 
        > Likelihood ratio test=3.56  on 2 df, p=0.169  n= 92 
        > 
        > BUT: 
        >  > 2*(1-pnorm(0.814))
        > [1] 0.415645
        > 
        > This p-value is different than one listed by the original output.

        Only by rounding the output.  The code in S-PLUS 3.4 and 5.1 is 

                        tmp <- cbind(coef, exp(coef), se, coef/se, signif(1
-
        pchisq((coef/se)^2, 1), digits - 1))

        What value do you have options(digits) set at?  If you have 7, 
        digits is 3 and so you have 2 significant figures.

        I really think this arbitrary manipulation of precision in the
survival
        routines is crazy, but after ten years' of complaining have given up
on
        it.

        --

messages.subject: RE: p-value in coxph
messages.body_plain:
Given what I know about data, models, and assumptions, I find more than
2 significant digits of printout for a p-value to be indefensible.  (I actually
think 1 digit is about the max).  

   In coxph, the way that I trimmed the number of digits wasn't too wise;
the anomaly that you pointed out is the most non-intuitive of several issues.
Brian is right, it should be changed.  In fact, it's been on my list for a
long while (I actually do listen to him -- on rare ocassions he's right :-),
but when I'll make the fix, in the face of dozens of other enhancements,
is uncertain.

  What I intend to do -- make the p-value printout always take up 5 characters
of output, with "<.001" as the string for the small ones.  Apply the formatting
rules only to the default output, so that those who want more digits can
type  (summary(fit))$table, to see it using "standard" Splus rules.

        Terry T.

messages.subject: RE: compressing objects
messages.body_plain:
There are several possible ways of handling this.

If your Win 2000 system is running on an NTFS file system, you could enable
Windows 2000 compression on the whole _Data directory (right-click on the
folder in explorer).  That would be the easiest.  If you don't want to
compress the whole directory, use object names that comply with the 8+3
(nnnnnnnn.xxx) naming system.  Then you'll recognize which data objects
correspond with which files.  You could then compress individual objects.
This will be transparent to S-Plus.

If you stick with 8+3 names, you could move specific objects to a compressed
zip file and move them back when desired.  (This would be regardless of
whether you have an NTFS file system.)

If you have a zip drive, you could format it as NTFS and enable compression.
You could then create an S-plus data directory there and attach it to your
session.  Move some of the big objects over.  Re-create them in your working
directory when you need them.

  - Lane

messages.subject: Re: submatrices
messages.body_plain:
"Duin, R.N.M." <R.N.M.Duin at rikz.rws.minvenw.nl> writes:

> I have a question about creating submatrices of a big matrix
> without using loops. My main interest lies in doing statistics
> (just mean and number of values without missing values) on
> submatrices. [...]

Assume x is an m-by-n matrix than can be divided into p-by-q
blocks, and you want to perform som operation on each block,
resulting in a scalar value (one for each block), resulting in an
m/p-by-n/q matrix.  Then the following will convert x into an
m/p*n/q-by-p*q matrix where each row contains the elements of each
submatrix

   m <- nrow(x)                         # number of rows
   n <- ncol(x)                         # number of columns
   dim(x) <- c(p, m/p, q, n/q)          # reshape the array
   x <- aperm(x, c(2, 4, 1, 3))         # permute the dimensions
   dim(x) <- c(m/p*n/q, p*q)            # reshape again

Now you can easily perform any operation you like (mean, median,
max, min, etc.) on each row to get a m/p*n/q-by-1 vector.  For
instance, to compute the mean of each submatrix:

   out <- x %*% rep(1/(p*q), p*q)

Of course, for other operations, you might need a loop treating
each row separately.  Finally, convert to the m/p-by-n/q matrix.

   dim(out) <- c(m/p, n/q)

There, now you have computed the mean (assuming the example above)
of each block.

Peter

-- 
Peter J. Acklam - jacklam at math.uio.no - http://www.math.uio.no/~jacklam

messages.subject: Re: Data analysis of Florida, USA voting patterns
messages.subject_clean: Data analysis of Florida, USA voting patterns
messages.body_plain:
I am quite interested in seeing continuing discussion of the statistical
issues related to understanding and interpreting the election results.  This
is an issue that demands sound statistical reasoning and inputs.

The past year saw a rejection of the idea of stratified sampling as a basis
for US census counting.  We are now seeing many alternative interpretations
of basic reported election data.  The election of the US president and
determination of what constitutes "significant" or "material" distortion of
the will of the electorate are very real world applications for good
statistical reasoning.

The past year also saw the death of John Tukey who once said:     "The best
thing about being a statistician, is that you get to play in everyone's
backyard."  ( I only mention this because this may seem like a US issue and
sometimes S-News seems like a place where a couple of guys from Australia
and the UK help the rest of us see the light.)

I have just been watching a CNN reporter asking a campaign official why he
would argue with the official count.  Obviously, the reporter hasn't seen
the graphs and data as available on s-news.  To add another issue to those
that already have been raised on the list, analysis of the re-count changes
can provide some interesting insights into what represents a significant
distortion or an event that needs an explanation.  One source for Florida
recount data is
http://www.foxnews.com/elections/florida_recount.html
This data appears to contain significant "signal" but the implications could
benefit from the statistical expertise of the participants of this list at
interpretation and graphical presentation.

I look forward to continuing posts to this list from people adding analysis
and insights to illuminating election issues.

\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\
Dan Rie
Scituate, MA

messages.subject: simple regression question
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have measured 5 energies with a spectrometer.  There is noise on the
data and I have many measurements of each of the 5 energies, each with
an error bar.  To first order, it is obvious how to fit:

lm( measured.energy ~ energy.factor, weights=1/measured.energy.errors^2, 
data=spec.dat )

where spec.dat$energy.factor is a factor that designates different
energies.

Now the overall calibration factor of the spectrometer, which appears
as a global factor in all 5 energies, may depend on temperature,
humidity, and date in a linear way, i.e. K = K0 + a1 * temperature +
a2 * humidity + a3 * date.  I'd like to fit these data to get these
coefficients.  My data sheet contains columns for date, humidity, and
temperature in addition to the energies.  I envision this as an 8
parameter fit: 5 energies plus coefficients for date, humidity, and
temperature.

My question is, what is the correct way to specify this model for lm?

                               Thanks,
                                Scott

messages.subject: Re: nonlinear model parameter estimation
messages.body_plain:
Hi Shareef,

we (at the Danish Instiitute for FIsheries Research) use AD Model Builder as
well as S-plus (or R). For large problems with more than 30 parameters we
would never use the optimisation in S-plus or R directly, as all kinds of
numerical issues arise. We have used AD Model Builder for estimation in
non-linear fish stock assessment problems with up to 100 parameters.
Computing time for fitting parameters in these models were up to 1 minute on
a 450 MHz PC with plenty of RAM. In our experience, that is about the best
performance one can get.

We often do the subsequent data analysis and graphics in R or S-plus, which
works really well. We interchange data between R and AD Model Builder using
plain ASCII files, which is fast to program and robust. We are also trying
to get the DLL mechanism up and running, where ADMB compiles to a DLL which
then works as integrated in R as an internal routine. This is quite a nifty
idea, but do expect to mess a bit about with compiler specifics ;-)

Good luck. Cheers,

Uffe

A less sophisticated statistical analysis (OLS regression) with Excel plots

I have no clue as what will occur legally, but it is pretty awesome to think

pretty awesome to realize that the presidential election may end up electing
the wrong person due to an aberration that caused a few hundred folks in one
county in Florida to mistakenly cast their votes for the wrong person or to
invalidate their ballots of several thousand others (but still a tiny
percentage) by causing them to incorrectly vote twice.

Dear QIANG,
You can use the following function to compute
the correlation between 2 vectors x & y with
missing data.

cor.hm <- function(x,y) {

# Statement to give the subscripts of x: 
# Non missing (ok) values in x:
if(len(x)!=len(y)){
  print("Error in cor(x,y): lengths must be equal")
} 
if(len(x)==len(y)){
   x.ok <- (1:len(x))[!is.na(x)] 

   # Repeat the statement for y:
   y.ok <- (1:len(y))[!is.na(y)]     

   # Gives the positions (1:len(x)) that have data in both x and y
   ok <- y.ok[match(x.ok,y.ok,nomatch=0)] 
   cor(x[ok],y[ok])}
} 

This function works fine.
I have been using it for several years.
Have a nice day,
Mostafa El Hamly

messages.subject: RE: Florida votes
messages.body_plain:
>From a statistician's perspective, this election has been as much fun as I
could possibly have hoped for.  I have enjoyed the comments and discussions
by the members of the mailing list.

We have seen that Palm Beach county has a voting pattern that is surprising,
perhaps unexpected.  But in analyzing the results of the election, an
important question to address is: "What was the expected outcome of the
election."  (Preferably answered before the election.)  Then consider if the
observed outcome is different from what was expected.

For example:

Are the 19,000+ invalidated ballots an outlier in Florida?  Perhaps so with
respect to other counties in this election.  Perhaps not with respect to
earlier elections in this county.

Is the relatively high vote count for Buchanan in Palm Beach county
unexpected?  Perhaps compared to other counties in the state of Florida, but
perhaps not relative to voter registration records.  (Based on a quick
calculation from 1998 registration records available at
  http://www.leg.state.fl.us/edr/voters.htm
about 18% of voters registered as independents - not an obvious outlier).

I guess what I'm trying to say is that all the analyses of this election
will to greater or lesser extent be biased by a hypothesis of what "should"
have happened, and the choice of the "prior" hypothesis may have more
influence on the analysis than the data.

Watching the saga unfold,

Kevin Wright

messages.body_plain:
The following might be interest for those following press coverage of the
possible role of statistics in this dispute.  (The printed version in the
edition I receive contained additional comments by David Freedman, also
downplaying the potential of statistics in this highly charged situation.
I would not follow Persi very far on the analogy to census undercount
adjustment, since anything that would be done now on the elections would
be post hoc and supported by little research, which is different from
the census situation ... but that's another discussion!)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------
IN RESEARCH, RECOUNTS ARE NORM
http://www.nytimes.com/2000/11/10/politics/10MATH.html

November 10, 2000
THE SCIENCE OF COUNTING
By GINA KOLATA

First George W. Bush led Al Gore by 1,784 votes in Florida. Then, an
unofficial count by The Associated Press suggested his lead was slashed
to less than half that. So, which number is right mathematically?

Statisticians chuckled at the idea.

"There's always going to be an error," said Howard Wainer, a statistician
at the Educational Testing Service in Princeton, N.J.  "Every time you
count them, you're going to get a different answer."

In research, said Diana C. Mutz, a professor of political science at Ohio
State University, scientists will repeat a process multiple times and
choose a number somewhere in the middle of their data as most likely to
reflect the truth. But, she and others said, multiple recounts are
probably not desirable in the presidential election because they would
add to the delay and uncertainty, not to say the bickering. Whoever was
losing could argue for one more recount.

Even if it were just a research question, Professor Mutz was not sure how
many counts would be needed to make her confident the Florida vote was as
accurate as it could be. How many times she would count it "depends on
how many graduate students I have," she joked.

Then there is the problem of Palm Beach County, Fla., where residents
said confusion over the ballot led more than 19,000 voters in a heavily
Democratic area to mark two candidates instead of one for president.
Their ballots were discarded as invalid. And, adding to the confusion,
Patrick J. Buchanan won more than 3,000 votes in Palm Beach. Some
Democrats said many people accidentally voted for Mr. Buchanan when they
meant to vote for Mr. Gore. Isn't there a way to fix that? A statistical
adjustment, perhaps?

Sorry, say the statisticians. Any adjustment would only make matters
worse. Persi Diaconis, a statistician at Stanford University, said the
situation reminded him of attempts to adjust the census to correct for
the undercount, the people who were missed. The census recount turned out
to be a nightmare, he said, with new errors introduced and even more
squabbling.

"The process really degenerates," Professor Diaconis said. "It's not at
all simple."
      
Copyright 2000 The New York Times Company

messages.subject: Data is/are
messages.body_plain:
The number of "data" is almost an FAQ.  Here are a few sources for
American English usage.  I believe that British English tends to more
use of the plural with collective nouns ("Manchester United have excellent
goaltending") while American English tends to more use of the singular
("General Motors has surpassed previous earnings), and that, as well as
perhaps a lesser regard for Latin origins on my side of the Atlantic,
may be driving some of the usage differences.  (In the interests of full
disclosure, I personally prefer "The data are ...")

---------------------------------------------------------------------------
Webster's dictionary (1913 edition, see
http://humanities.uchicago.edu/forms_unrest/webster.form.html):  "Data"
is plural of "datum".
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
Merriam-Webster dictionary (see http://www.m-w.com/cgi-bin/dictionary):
"Function: noun plural but singular or plural in construction ...
Usage: Data leads a life of its own quite independent of datum, of which
it was originally the plural. It occurs in two constructions: as a plural
noun (like earnings), taking a plural verb and plural modifiers (as
these, many, a few) but not cardinal numbers, and serving as a referent
for plural pronouns (as they, them); and as an abstract mass noun (like
information), taking a singular verb and singular modifiers (as this,
much, little), and being referred to by a singular pronoun (it). Both
constructions are standard. The plural construction is more common in
print, evidently because the house style of several publishers mandates it."
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

One of several articles at www.dictionary.com:

pl.n. attributive. 
[Latin, pl. of datum; see datum.] 

Usage Note: Data originated as the plural of Latin datum, "something
given," and many maintain that it must still be treated as a plural form.
The New York Times, for example, adheres to the traditional rule in this
headline: "Data Are Elusive on the Homeless." But while data comes from a
Latin plural form, the practice of treating data as a plural in English
often does not correspond to its meaning, given an understanding of what
counts as data in modern research. We know, for example, what "data on
the homeless" would consist ofsurveys, case histories, statistical
analyses, and so forthbut it would be a vain exercise to try to sort all
of these out into sets of individual facts, each of them a "datum" on the
homeless. (Does a case history count as a single datum, or as a
collection of them? Is a correlation between rates of homelessness and
unemployment itself a datum, or is it an abstraction over a number of
data?) Since scientists and researchers think of data as a singular mass
entity like information, it is entirely natural that they should have
come to talk about it as such and that others should defer to their
practice. Sixty percent of the Usage Panel accepts the use of data with a
singular verb and pronoun in the sentence "Once the data is in, we can
begin to analyze it." A still larger number, 77 percent, accepts the
sentence "We have very little data on the efficacy of such programs," where
the singularity of data is implicit in the use of the quantifier very
little (contrast the oddness of We have very little facts on the efficacy
of such programs).

Source: The American Heritage Dictionary of the English Language, Third
Edition Copyright  1996, 1992 by Houghton Mifflin Company.

[After you read this, please don't write to me about British/American 
practices on placing commas inside/outside the quotation marks!]

messages.subject: The number of ``data''.
messages.body_plain:
The unfortunate trend of accepting ``data'' as a singular noun is an
aspect of the general sloppiness and dumbing down of English usage
along with most other areas of intelectual activity.  This general
trend is encouraged and exacerbated by the prevailing terror of being
politically incorrect or ``damaging someone's self esteem'' [see
footnote].

I am reminded of a Doonsbury cartoon wherein a character (with
reference to the square root of 144) says ``My culture teaches that
it's 15, man!''

The word ``data'' is plural.  The phrase ``data set'' is singular.
If you mean ``data set'' say so, and don't be sloppy and mentally
lazy.

                                        cheers,

                                                Rolf Turner
                                                rolf at math.unb.ca

Footnote:  Self esteem --- Italian for sauna.

messages.subject: Data is/are
messages.body_plain:
I hesitate to step into this debate, but while it's clear the Pluricans
have etymology on their side, the Singulacrats have usage (and a good
deal of history) on theirs. Some examples: 

- If etymology counted for everything, we'd still say "My stamina aren't
what they once were", for instance. 

- One naturally regards "data" as an aggregate, where the whole is
perceived more readily than the parts. Applying the singular seems
appropriate when we primarily see a distinct entity rather than its
components. We say "Sugar is sweet and sand is brown", not "Sugar are
sweet and sand are brown". And even though it would be grammatical, we
rarely have need to say "Sugars are sweet and sands are brown." 

- We've seen a simlilar historical shift with "news", as in this old
newspaper joke: Q. "Any news?" A. "Not a single damn new."

Although it's safer to stick to the plural in formal writing, it's
difficult to argue that people who use the singular are making a
grammatical error of the same order as, say, its/it's.

-- 
Kieran Healy, 
Department of Sociology, Princeton University      
Princeton, NJ 08544. kjhealy at princeton.edu

messages.body_plain:
From  Merriam
Webster Online Dictionary

                
Main Entry: da·ta

                
Pronunciation: 'dA-t&, 'da- also 'dä-

                
Function: noun plural but singular or plural in construction

                
Usage: often attributive

                
Etymology: Latin, plural of datum

                
Date: 1646

                
1 : factual information (as measurements or statistics) used as a basis

                
for reasoning, discussion, or calculation <the data is plentiful and
easily

                
available -- H. A. Gleason, Jr.> <comprehensive data on economic

                
growth have been published -- N. H. Jacoby>

                
2 : information output by a sensing device or organ that includes both

                
useful and irrelevant or redundant information and must be processed

                
to be meaningful

                
3 : information in numerical form that can be digitally transmitted or

                
processed

                
usage Data leads a life of its own quite independent of datum, of

                
which it was originally the plural. It occurs in two constructions:
as a

                
plural noun (like earnings), taking a plural verb and plural modifiers
(as

                
these, many, a few) but not cardinal numbers, and serving as a

                
referent for plural pronouns (as they, them); and as an abstract mass

                
noun (like information), taking a singular verb and singular modifiers

                
(as this, much, little), and being referred to by a singular pronoun (it).

                
Both constructions are standard. The plural construction is more

                
common in print, evidently because the house style of several

                
publishers mandates it.

messages.subject: Summary: Compressing Objects
messages.body_plain:
Thanks to Lane Bishop, Vadim Ogranovich, Don McKenzie, Hong Ooi, and Ray
Falk for their advice on how to clean up some of my disk space by
compressing and/or removing currently-unneeded objects.  Everyone's
inputs are below, with the solution that worked for me at the end.

FROM LANE:
If your Win 2000 system is running on an NTFS file system, you could
enable
Windows 2000 compression on the whole _Data directory.That would be the
easiest.  If you don't want to compress the whole directory, use object
names that comply with the 8+3(nnnnnnnn.xxx) naming system.  Then you'll
recognize which data objects correspond with which files.  You could
then compress individual objects. This will be transparent to S-Plus.
If you stick with 8+3 names, you could move specific objects to a
compressed zip file and move them back when desired.  (This would be
regardless of whether you have an NTFS file system.)  If you have a zip
drive, you could format it as NTFS and enable compression.  You could
then create an S-plus data directory there and attach it to your
session.  Move some of the big objects over.  Re-create them in your
working directory when you need them.

(NOTE: THE 8+3 NAMES MUST BE LOWER CASE)

Others have suggested not to use Windows utilities to move S-Plus
objects
around - that is probably good advice.  You might prefer to stick to
either
compressing the whole directory, or creating a new one for your archived
large objects, using S-Plus tools to move the objects there, and then
compressing or zipping up that whole directory.  It might be better to
stick
to the S-plus tools to move things around - although I have not had
trouble
in the past.  (You do need to detach and re-attach a directory if you
add an
object manually.)

FROM VADIM:
It seems like formatting zip drive to NTFS can severely hurt
access speed, especially for writing. I had this problem with my Jaz
drive.
Iomega support help explicitly "does not recommend nor support NTFS
format"
on (Jaz) drives.

FROM DON:
One thing you can do is use data.dump() to create ascii versions (with
names that you choose).  Then delete (temporarily) the corresponding S
objects and store the ascii versions on the zip (preferably somewhere
else
also though because zips have a non-zero failure rate).  When you need
them again, use data.restore() on the ascii objects.
e.g. >
data.dump("big.useless.matrix",file="my.zip.drive/biguselessmatrix")

I've been told that problems can arise when you move things in and out
of
_Data using Windows utilities.  The internal record that S keeps of the
objects in this directory gets corrupted.  One might want to check this
out with Mathsoft before proceeding.

FROM RAY:
S+ includes a true.file.name() function, which returns the "dumb" coded
name
for an s+ object
> true.file.name(xyz)
__234

This may be applied to a list of object names
> mySTAR.true.file.names <- true.file.name(objects(pattern="my*"))
__123 mycap mylung my.function1 my.func2

or

> mySTARdata.true.file.names <- true.file.name(dimnames(objects.summary(
        
pattern="my*",data.class="data.frame"))[[1]])
__123 mycap mylung

etc.

Of course, the best way of controlling is through the search path
(to which others might respond better than I.

MY SOLUTION:
I used Lane's suggestion and renamed the objects in the Object Explorer
to the 8.3 convention using lower case letters and numbers.  This did
indeed change the name of the object files from their funky version
(e.g. _834) to the name of the object so I knew which files to compress.
After some testing, I found that I could use the Windows Zip utility to
compress several files into a .zip file.  While zipped, S-PLUS did not
recognize the files.  But it did recognize them with no problems after
they were unzipped.  I achieved over 90% compression with this.  I did
some other testing and found that I could not move the object files in
and out of the directory using Windows and have S-PLUS recognize it when
I moved it back in.  So, if anyone uses my method, make sure you leave
the .zip file in the working directory and unzip the files to the same
directory.  If I keep everything in the same directory, S-PLUS is happy.

Win

messages.subject: stepwise, leaps and stepAIC
messages.body_plain:
S-PLUS 2000 Windows 2000

Okay, here's the deal.  I have to automate the development of 276 linear
regression equations, or I will age beyond my years.  I am doing this in
blocks of 72 to keep things more organized.  I have ~200 potential
predictors to choose from for each equation.  In all my individual tests
I used stepwise() because the input is easy to provide and the output is
easy to understand.  It was easy to go through the 'which' object and
see which predictors were chosen and in what order, then slowly build a
linear regression model and test it on an independent (training) data
set.  I cut off the addition of new predictors when the change in
r-squared became less than 0.5% in lm(), which typically occurred after
4 or 5 predictors.

leaps() and stepAIC() both look like promising prospects, but their
inputs do not look appealing.  I have the predictand and predictors in
one dataframe.  The call I gave to stepwise looked like

>stepwise(DF[,2:200], DF[,1])

where DF[,2:200] are the predictors in columns 2-200, and DF[,1] is the
predictand in column 1.  leaps() takes the same inputs with a few others
I will have to figure out before I add them.  stepAIC() requires a basic
model ('object' in help), and the 'scope' defining a range of models.
It would be highly inconvenient to type out the max model with ~200
possible predictors.

I would like to know:
1.  What some of you think of leaps() (it wasn't highly touted in MASS)
2.  Is there a better way to define the max model in stepAIC()?
3.  Are there any other suggestions than those I've proposed here?

Thanks much.

messages.subject: Data is/are pedantics
messages.body_plain:
My apologies for unintentionally starting a war!  This whole discussion is
off-topic and this will be my last message about it.  In response to others'
comments/questions in no particular order:

- I was referencing the Merriam-Webster's New Collegiate Dictionary (print
version) which says exactly what many have quoted from the online version.

- There are obviously many usage differences among US/Canadian/UK/Australian
and other English dialects.  The OED is not an authority on American usage.
As someone noted, either Webster's or Random House is usually considered the
standard for American usage.    (An American student spelling aluminum with
two i's, aluminium, would be marked wrong.)

- Another authority, The Elements of Style by Strunk and White (1979),
agrees with Webster's that singular usage is gaining acceptance.  That
source also includes strata, phenomena, and media as other examples of
singular usage growing acceptance. ("The media is/are reporting on the
recent election results" are both heard here in the US.)

- I tried the MS Word style check as suggested below after setting the
language to UK, Canadian, Australian, and with several other dialects.  All
passed both "The data is messy" and "The data are messy."

- I could point out that there are more of us that speak American English,
but I won't

- My preference would also be "The data are ..."  I was merely pointing out
that either phrasing is considered correct.

> From: s-news-owner at lists.biostat.wustl.edu
> [mailto:s-news-owner at lists.biostat.wustl.edu]On Behalf Of Cunningham,

> Subject: [S] Re: The Data {is,are}
>
>

>
> I typed:
>       The data are messy.  The data is messy.
>

messages.subject_clean: Sequential sums of squares from poly()
messages.body_plain:
At 10:46 10/11/00 -0700, Greg Snow wrote:

>

>If I fit a model like:

>eth.fit <- lm( NOx ~ poly(E,8), data=Ethanol )

>

>then do a summary, it gives a t-test for each parameter, but if I do:A

>anova(eth.fit), then it groups all 8 parameters and does 1 test of all the

>parameters at the same time.  Is there a way to get the sequential sums of

>squares for the 8 different parameters without entering each one

>seperately in the formula?

>

>I know that since poly creates orthogonal polynomials the t-tests are

>equivalent to the sequential tests, but I would like the sequential table

>that comes from anova with one object, and the same would apply for a

>matrix term that is not orthogonal.

Multiple degrees-of-freedom factor terms in linear models can be split into components using the "split" option of summary.aov, but I don't know of any automatic way of splitting non-factor terms  sequentially into single degree-or-freedom terms like this.

Essentially you have to pass on to the terms parser the information that you want the columns of the matrix to be treated as separate regressors.  There are, of course, fairly simple indirect ways of doing this and for your example above one way would be as follows:

> names(ethanol)

[1] "NOx" "C"   "E"  

> attach(ethanol)

> X <- data.frame(poly(E, 8))

> names(X)

[1] "X1" "X2" "X3" "X4" "X5" "X6" "X7" "X8"

> eth <- cbind(ethanol, X)

> fm <- aov(NOx ~ .-E-C, eth)

> summary(fm)

Df Sum of Sq  Mean Sq  F Value     Pr(F) 

X1  1   1.15491  1.15491  10.4594 0.0017822

X2  1  85.75875 85.75875 776.6711 0.0000000

X3  1   0.23803  0.23803   2.1557 0.1460154

X4  1  13.20688 13.20688 119.6076 0.0000000

X5  1   0.83221  0.83221   7.5369 0.0074813

X6  1   1.31765  1.31765  11.9333 0.0008896

X7  1   0.28614  0.28614   2.5914 0.1114356

X8  1   0.10620  0.10620   0.9618 0.3297328

Residuals 79   8.72305  0.11042                   

> 

There is the table you wanted, but I guess the answer to this question is really "no, not easily".

messages.subject: Re: Data is/are
messages.body_plain:
The odd thing about living in Australia is that you sleep when most of the
English-speaking world is awake and conversely.  This was one of the
mornings when I woke up to find that a grammar war had broken out and had
been progress for much of the night, and it was started by none other than
Madeline "stirrer" Bauer.  I had no idea she had such a devilish sense of
fun...(well, maybe some idea).   I can't resist tossing in a couple of
comments, even if you have all gone to bed by now, worn out by battle fatigue.

This "data is/are" issue will never be settled, that much is clear.  The
Australian OXFORD dictionary, by the way, accepts both singular and plural
for "data" (which doesn't bother me greatly), but then it also accepts
"alternate" and "alternative" as synonyms and that just about made me want
to toss it away.  (Next it will be recognizing m/d/y as a legitimate form
for dates and not the mongrel bastard of a thing that it is.)

Whether the word is singular or plural, when a statistician speaks of
"data" it really is (or should be) a singular concept.  We think of data as
the full set of information on which an analysis is based, logically a
seamless whole that has to be handled in toto, not as a collection of
loosely linked entities from which pieces can be selected more-or-less at
will for analysis (as some clinets or even colleagues often want us to do).
 I think this is very important to keep in mind.  

The other point that stikes me as strange is the usage "data analysis".
When we use a noun as an adjective in English it is usually (and as far as
I am concerned, always) the singular form.  It's "a horse doctor" not "a
horses doctor" and "a mouse plague" not "a mice plague", even though
presumably the doctor can tend more than one animal and one mouse does not
make much of a plague.  Does anyone want to change and start calling it
"datum analysis"?  Might be fun.

For some reason I cannot help wincing, though, when people do mistakenly
use the plural Latin or Greek form when the singular is intended, available
and in widespread use.  Examples that do it for me are "strata" and
"bacteria" (Latin) and "criteria" and "phenomena" (Greek).  "media" is
right on the border.   Precede any of these with the indefinite article,
"a", in my hearing and I will get an almost uncontrollable urge to correct
you.  It has proved awkward and embarrassing at times.

There are good examples, though, of the plural Latin form  becoming a fully
idiomatic singular form in English, such as "stamina" and "agenda".  In
fact I think of the usage of "agenda" as pretty close to that of "data" in
the way it can function as singular or plural.  It is occasionally used in
a plural sense, and agendum is still in common usage for one item "on
(of?) the agenda", but there are plenty of idioms where it is used with a
singular sense without raising any flak from the grammar squad.  In fact
this is the norm and there is even some evidence that "agenda" had already
started to attract a singular sense even in Latin speaking times.

I love this kind of stuff and I could go on and on, but I guess that's
enough (at least for now...)

Bill Venables

At 15:16 10/11/00 -0500, Kieran Healy wrote:
>I hesitate to step into this debate, but while it's clear the Pluricans
>have etymology on their side, the Singulacrats have usage (and a good
>deal of history) on theirs. Some examples: 
>
>- If etymology counted for everything, we'd still say "My stamina aren't
>what they once were", for instance. 
>
>- One naturally regards "data" as an aggregate, where the whole is
>perceived more readily than the parts. Applying the singular seems
>appropriate when we primarily see a distinct entity rather than its
>components. We say "Sugar is sweet and sand is brown", not "Sugar are
>sweet and sand are brown". And even though it would be grammatical, we
>rarely have need to say "Sugars are sweet and sands are brown." 
>
>- We've seen a simlilar historical shift with "news", as in this old
>newspaper joke: Q. "Any news?" A. "Not a single damn new."
>
>Although it's safer to stick to the plural in formal writing, it's
>difficult to argue that people who use the singular are making a
>grammatical error of the same order as, say, its/it's.
>
>-- 
>Kieran Healy, 
>Department of Sociology, Princeton University      
>Princeton, NJ 08544. kjhealy at princeton.edu

messages.body_plain:
At 18:09 10/11/00 -0500, Winifred Lambert wrote:
>S-PLUS 2000 Windows 2000
>
>Okay, here's the deal.  

"The deal"?  I'm stumped.

>I have to automate the development of 276 linear
>regression equations, or I will age beyond my years.  I am doing this in
>blocks of 72 to keep things more organized.  I have ~200 potential
>predictors to choose from for each equation.  In all my individual tests
>I used stepwise() because the input is easy to provide and the output is
>easy to understand.  It was easy to go through the 'which' object and
>see which predictors were chosen and in what order, then slowly build a
>linear regression model and test it on an independent (training) data
>set.  I cut off the addition of new predictors when the change in
>r-squared became less than 0.5% in lm(), which typically occurred after
>4 or 5 predictors.
>
>leaps() and stepAIC() both look like promising prospects, but their
>inputs do not look appealing.  I have the predictand and predictors in
>one dataframe.  The call I gave to stepwise looked like
>
>>stepwise(DF[,2:200], DF[,1])
>
>where DF[,2:200] are the predictors in columns 2-200, and DF[,1] is the
>predictand in column 1.  leaps() takes the same inputs with a few others
>I will have to figure out before I add them.  stepAIC() requires a basic
>model ('object' in help), and the 'scope' defining a range of models.
>It would be highly inconvenient to type out the max model with ~200
>possible predictors.
>
>I would like to know:
>1.  What some of you think of leaps() (it wasn't highly touted in MASS)

According to my help info, leaps can only take up 31 predictors, so it's
not available for your problem.

leaps() performs a well-defined computation and I don't think we have any
particular objection to what it does.    You should not read too much into
what is not in MASS: that just as often as not reflects space constraints. 

>2.  Is there a better way to define the max model in stepAIC()?

If your DF is a data frame, you could actually construct the formula
without typing very much at all.  Here is a sketch of how you might go
about it:

f.lower <- paste(names(DF)[1], "~", 1)
f.upper <- paste(names(DF)[1], "~", paste(names(DF)[-1], collapse = " + "))

f0 <- lm(f.lower, DF)
f.step <- stepAIC(f0, list(upper = f.upper, lower = f.lower), trace = F)

Note that in a couple of places here instead of a formula you can use a
character string that parses to a formula.  This is handy in this kind of
situation.

>3.  Are there any other suggestions than those I've proposed here?

stepAIC will in all probability be pretty slow, but if you can put your
computations through a For() loop (as opposed to a for() loop) it might be
manageable.  AIC is known to be a pretty lenient criterion, too.  You might
want to tighten up the complexity penalty a bit (the "k" argument to
stepAIC) if you want more parsimonious selection.

What other techniques you might adopt depend very much on the context of
what you are doing.  If you are just after a prediction equation it *could*
be the case that tree models do a pretty good job and after pruning they
are usually pretty economical in the predictors they use.    Then again,
they could be terrible.  Partial least squares and the lasso are also often
mooted as pretty good alternatives to explicit variable selection, but
whether they are suitable for your problem is something only you can say at
this stage.

messages.subject: US Election results
messages.body_plain:
Is there any source available that breaks down the US votes by 
congressional district on a state-by-state basis?  I ask because Nebraska 
and Maine have creative systems for awarding electoral votes.  I'd like to 
see whether a national version of the Nebraska/Maine system would have made 
a significant difference in the present election.

For those unfamiliar with the Maine/Nebraska system, electoral votes are 
awarded as follows:

Votes are tallied by congressional district.  The candidate who wins the 
congressional district is awarded that district's one electoral vote.  The 
statewide winner (in popular vote) is awarded the 2 electoral votes 
corresponding to the Senate seats.  The only way a candidate can win all 
the state's electoral votes is to win in every congressional district.

messages.subject: Definition of BIC: factor of -2 or not?
messages.subject_clean: Definition of BIC: factor of -2 or not?
messages.body_plain:
I've noticed that S-Plus uses the definition of BIC as
(1)     -2 loglikelihood + (number of parameters)*log(sample size)
Others (like my sociologists co-author's idol) use
(2)     loglikelihood - 1/2 (number of parameters)*log(sample size)

Obviously either will do as long as one is consistent, but is there 
any compelling reason (historical, cultural, . . . ) to prefer one to 
the other?

Put another way, what sort of people use (1) and what sort of people 
use (2)? Number (2) matches Schwarz's use, so why does S-Plus use (1)?

Steve Buyske

messages.body_plain:
At 19:40 11/11/00 -0500, Steve Buyske wrote:
>I've noticed that S-Plus uses the definition of BIC as
>(1)    -2 loglikelihood + (number of parameters)*log(sample size)
>Others (like my sociologists co-author's idol) use
>(2)    loglikelihood - 1/2 (number of parameters)*log(sample size)
>
>Obviously either will do as long as one is consistent, but is there 
>any compelling reason (historical, cultural, . . . ) to prefer one to 
>the other?
>Put another way, what sort of people use (1) and what sort of people 
>use (2)? Number (2) matches Schwarz's use, so why does S-Plus use (1)?

Here's a guess.  

-2 log(likelihood) by itself is the quantity for which differences
represent approximate chi-squared tests, so if you look at differences only
the first represents something closer to the sorts of quantities
statisticians are used to working with.  (Note that neither is uniquely
defined.  log(likelihood) is only defined up to an arbitrary additive
constant  and so only differences are meaningful.)

Note, too, that many optimisation algorithms settle on minimisation as the
paradigm rather than maximisation.  I don't really know why this is, but I
can't help suspecting that psychologically minimisation *seems* easier than
maximisation purely because of the way gravity tends subliminally to play a
part in our thinking.  For the first definition you minimise BIC and for
the second you maximise it.  The second seems much harder going and the
consequences of slipping along the way much more serious...  :-)

Bill Venables.

messages.body_plain:
On Sun, 12 Nov 2000, Vadim Ogranovich wrote:

> During the time I've been hanging on the list I've seen multiple discussions
> regarding step-wise regression and no one regarding Bayesian Model Averaging
> (BMA) which, in my understanding, claims to be a better technique for
> dealing with the cases where the number of observations is not that much
> bigger than the number of possible regression variables.
> Is there a good reason why people stay away from BMA?

I mentioned shrinkage methods in a recent post: this is another shrinkage
method (a computationally expensive one) with a rather peculiar prior,
from the shrinkage point of view.

> Thanks, Vadim
> 
> P.S. As far as I know there is some public S software on Statlib which does
> Monte-Carlo Model Averaging, though I never tried it.

Which did you have in mind?   There's bicreg, which uses the (rather crude)
BIC approximation, and bma which `perform Bayesian simultaneous variable
selection and outlier identification via Markov chain Monte Carlo model
composition'.  Both seem to me to do model selection, not model averaging
per se.

One problem here is that one group within what is a large field has
appropriated the term BMA, although others argue that their work is neither
B nor A.  There have been Bayesian model averaging approaches for a long
time, as Geisser's 1993 book (for example) points out.

messages.body_plain:
On Sat, 11 Nov 2000, Steve Buyske wrote:

> I've noticed that S-Plus uses the definition of BIC as

`S-Plus uses'?  Given that there are inconsistent definitions
of AIC within S-PLUS, I wonder about BIC too.  Do you mean NLME?

> (1)   -2 loglikelihood + (number of parameters)*log(sample size)
> Others (like my sociologists co-author's idol) use
> (2)   loglikelihood - 1/2 (number of parameters)*log(sample size)
> 
> Obviously either will do as long as one is consistent, but is there 
> any compelling reason (historical, cultural, . . . ) to prefer one to 
> the other?
> Put another way, what sort of people use (1) and what sort of people 
> use (2)? Number (2) matches Schwarz's use, so why does S-Plus use (1)?

There are two 1978 sources for a criterion called `BIC', one by Akaike (who
did call it BIC) and one by Schwarz (who I am pretty sure did not, and in
any case only considered linear regression).  Time series people have
yet other variants.

Given that confusion, I tend to avoid the term.  More seriously, it is
derived by keeping some leading terms in a O(log n) asymptotic expansion,
and which terms to retain is debatable (and matters)  even in the
regression context.  (For example, Draper and Raftery retain different
sets, but both as I recall more than Schwarz.)  In the regression context
you don't need to approximate the expansion of the log determinant, anyway.  
In the NLME context, the asymptotics used by Schwarz look pretty strange.

Even worse, in a context of contingency tables, what is the sample size? It
seems to vary by model parameter, and it is easy to find examples where the
sample size is around a million, but only a few hundred points are
contributing to the estimation of the parameters of interest. For a
multi-level NLME, the effective sample size is unclear (although I know the
total number of observations is actually used).

A quick look on my shelf suggests that most of the books I have (and all I
sampled) which use `SBC' or `SIC' define it as (1).  I suspect that
in the spirit of Mallows' C_p,  a penalized sum of squares is easiest
to interpret.

--

messages.body_plain:
Hi Steve,

I think that most people using AIC and related information criteria
should read the book:
Burnham, K.P., Anderson, D.R., 1998. Model selection and inference: a
practical information-theoretic approach. New-York, Springer-Verlag, 353
p.
It gives a comprehensive presentation of Akaike's work and discusses
important issues such as model ranking, model selection uncertainty,
inference based on model averaging, etc. In the frame of
information-theoretic approach, the information criteria are relative
estimates of the Kullback-Liebler information: K-L = I(f, g), the
information lost when model g is used to approximate full reality f
("true model", always unknown). Quoting the authors:

BIC is in the family of "criteria that are consistent estimators of K,
the dimension of the 'true model'" (p.66)
[snip]
"BIC = - 2 * log (maximized likelihood) + K * log(n) (p. 68)
[where n is the sample size and K is the number of parameters]
BIC arises from a Bayesian viewpoint with equal priors on each model
and very vague priors on the parameters, given the model. The assumed
purpose of the BIC-selected model was often simple prediction; as
opposed to scientific understanding of the process or system under
study. BIC is not an estimator of the relative K-L."

>From my own experience, I found that BIC is often misleading (leads to
under-fitted models) when sample size is large, and stopped to use it.
Burnham and Anderson present criteria that can be used when sample size
is small (p. 51):
AICc = - 2 * log(maximized likelihood) + 2 * K * (n / (n - K - 1)

Hope this can help you,

Renaud

messages.subject: Re: Data is/are
messages.body_plain:
According to Bill Venables:
|> 
|> The odd thing about living in Australia is that you sleep when most of the
|> English-speaking world is awake and conversely.  This was one of the

It's even more so for those living in New Zealand.  Like Bill, I enjoy
this stuff which is not often well discussed.  Even though it's not
quiet a topic for this list, I'd like to put my oar in too.

|> .... and it was started by none other than
|> Madeline "stirrer" Bauer.  I had no idea she had such a devilish sense of
|> fun...(well, maybe some idea).   

It's interesting that nobody bit when she stated that "Data are
plural."  Was it that devilish sense of fun?  I think so.  She
undoubtedly would know that in English, only nouns, pronouns and verbs
can be plural.  Someone who was not joking would say:

"Data" is a plural noun.

Of course, there could be occasions when the data really are all nouns....

|> This "data is/are" issue will never be settled, that much is clear.  The
|> Australian OXFORD dictionary, by the way, accepts both singular and plural
|> for "data" (which doesn't bother me greatly), but then it also accepts
|> "alternate" and "alternative" as synonyms and that just about made me want
|> to toss it away.  (Next it will be recognizing m/d/y as a legitimate form
|> for dates and not the mongrel bastard of a thing that it is.)

:-) Bill usually has something illuminating and entertaining to add to
a discussion.

|> There are good examples, though, of the plural Latin form  becoming a fully
|> idiomatic singular form in English, such as "stamina" and "agenda".  

English is also strongly influenced by what gave rise to the German
language.  The similarities and differences between German and English
are interesting.  German, which is somewhat less mutable than English,
maintains characteristics that vanished from English centuries ago.
Someone more knowledgable than I could correct me on this, but from my
understanding of German, "information" refers to what in English would
be called "a piece of information".  "Information" has a plural in
German, not in English.  Somewhat similarly, politics can be referred
to individually. One of your politics could be in agreement with your
foes but all the rest can be opposed.  Maybe the English of yore used
to be more like that.  In any case, nowadays, politicians and
grammarians would nearly all agree that "Politics is a dirty
business".

"Data" is something like "information" and "politics".  One part of me
likes to keep the language similar to how previous generations used
it, but there are occasions when the changes are for the better.  To
have the word "data" come to refer to the collection rather than the
individual bits of information is not a bad change and loses nothing
that is an important distinction.

Like Kieran Healy, I find it much easier to keep my shirt on with this
lack of vocabulary or grammatical decorum than when I see/hear lack of
knowledge of the difference between it's/its.

I could make a long list before I got down to data is/are.  Some of
them include:

much/many
fewer/less
"you and I" (in the accusative case)
"you and me" (in the nominative case)
alot/a lot
to/too
hacker/cracker
adjective/adverb
alternate/alternative

OK.  I'll stop.

best

messages.subject: submatrices
messages.body_plain:
Dear all, what a fantastically medium snews is! Last week I posted a
question about calculating statistics for submatrices. The orginal question
was:

I have a question about creating submatrices of a big matrix without using
>loops. My main interest lies in doing statistics (just mean and number of
>values without missing values) on submatrices. The big matrix consists on
>measurements in blocks (e.g. depths within year and site) and I want to see
>what happens when the blocks are made bigger. So e.g. we have a matrix of
>8x8 and the first action  could be to investigate the behaviour of the 2x2
>non overlapping matrices. The second step could be 4x4 and eventually we
>have the whole matrix. Does anyone have some nice idea to make these
'moving
>windows' on matrices to work in splus. I do not see the solution in apply,
>because this function is only applicable on the whole column or row.
>
I get answers for this problems from Carlisle Thacker, Bill Dunlap (twice),
Tim Hesterberg and Peter Acklam. The answers are all different and therefore
I send them all for all whom interested in the same or related subject.
Again many thanks for your contribution.

********************************************************
* William Carlisle Thacker                             *
********************************************************
Have you tried flatteniing the matrix to a vector and combining it
into a dataframe with a "which" column, so you can use by() to build
the loops?

# make sample matrix
a <- matrix(1:64,ncol=8)

# make dataframe with columns indicating rows and columns of the matrix
flat <- data.frame(matrix = as.vector(a),
                      row = as.vector(row(a)), 
                      col = as.vector(col(a)))

# add column with indicator of which rows correspond to which 2x2
submatrices
# note magic number 2:  2x2 submatrices
# note magic number 4:  4x4 array of 2x2 submatrices

For such small matrices is a loopy solution really too slow?  E.g.,

blockApply <- function(x, blocksize, FUN, ...) {
        if(is.character(FUN)) FUN <- get(FUN, mode = "function")
        # in Splus5 use getFunction(FUN)
        if(nrow(x) %% blocksize != 0 || ncol(x) %% blocksize)
                stop("blocksize must divide nrow(x) and ncol(x)")
        val <- array(NA, c(dim(x)/blocksize))
        iseq <- ( - blocksize + 1):0
        for(i in 1:nrow(val)) {
                iseq <- iseq + blocksize
                jseq <- ( - blocksize + 1):0
                for(j in 1:ncol(val)) {
                        jseq <- jseq + blocksize
                        val[i, j] <- FUN(x[iseq, jseq], ...)
                }
        }
        val
}

On my pretty slow Sun with Splus 4 this takes about 5 seconds to calculate
the 64*64 minima of the 4 by 4 blocks in a 256 by 256 matrix.

> x<-matrix(sort(runif(256*256)), 256, 256)
> unix.time(blockApply(x,blocksize=4,min)->m4)
[1] 5.11000061 0.02999997 6.00000000 0.00000000 0.00000000

On this machine calling min(1) (or any other simple function)
64^2 times takes 0.42 seconds.  The rest of the time is for
manipulating the subscript expressions, additions, and : operator.

More efficiencies are possible, but it would take a while to
write the code.   The fastest would probably to use lapply()
and to use single subscripts instead of matrix subscripts.  I'm
not sure if you would get much better times even with that
approach.

Here is a version of blockApply that uses lapply and tries to do
most of the calculations before the iterations begin.  For some
simple functions it trims a third the time off the straightforward
version but as the function to be iterated gets more complicated
the benefits diminish.  It is considerably less readable.

blockApply2 <- function(x, blocksize, FUN, ...)
{
        if(is.character(FUN)) FUN <- get(FUN, mode = "function")
        # in Splus5 use getFunction(FUN)
        if(nrow(x) %% blocksize != 0 || ncol(x) %% blocksize)
                stop("blocksize must divide nrow(x) and ncol(x)")
        nrv <- dim(x)[1]/blocksize
        ncv <- dim(x)[2]/blocksize
        iseq0 <- 1:blocksize
        ijseq0 <- x[, iseq0]
        ijseq0[] <- seq(len = length(ijseq0))
        ijseq0 <- as.vector(ijseq0[1:blocksize,  ])
        val <- unlist(lapply(0:(nrv * ncv - 1), function(ij, x, nrowv,
nrowx, 
                ijseq0, blocksize, FUN, ...)
        FUN(x[ijseq0 + ij %% nrowv * blocksize + ij %/% nrowv * blocksize * 
                nrowx], ...), x, nrv, dim(x)[1], ijseq0, blocksize, FUN,
...))
        dim(val) <- c(nrv, ncv)
        val
}

Here x is a 300x10 matrix, and the final result is a matrix of the
sums of 2x2 non-overlapping matrices:

x _ matrix(runif(300*10), 300)
y _ matrix(fastColSums(x, 2, na.rm=T), ncol=10) # 10 = original # of columsn
t(matrix(fastColSums(t(y), 2, na.rm=T), 5))     # 5 = 10/2

To get number of non-missing values, repeat but with `x'
replaced by `!is.na(x)'.  Then divide to get means.
You can adapt this for any number other than 2.

This uses `fastColSums', which is a fast version of `colSums'
(which in turn is much faster than using `apply'), which has
an optional argument `n' which is used here in place of the actual
number of rows of the matrices.

fastColSums <-
function(x, n = numRows(x), na.rm = F)
{
  # Treat x as if it has n rows.
  # Use C code from colSums
  p <- length(x)/n
  COPY <- c(F, F, F, T, F, F)
  if(is.integer(x) || is.logical(x))
    .C("S_colSums_long_NA",
      as.integer(n),
      as.integer(p),
      x,
      answer = integer(p),
      na.rm = as.integer(na.rm),
      NAOK = T,
      specialsok = T,
      COPY = COPY[-5.])$answer
  else .C("S_colSums_NA",
      as.integer(n),
      as.integer(p),
      as.double(x),
      answer = double(p),
      divide = FALSE,
      na.rm = as.integer(na.rm),
      NAOK = T,
      specialsok = T,
      COPY = COPY)$answer
}

Assume x is an m-by-n matrix than can be divided into p-by-q
blocks, and you want to perform som operation on each block,
resulting in a scalar value (one for each block), resulting in an
m/p-by-n/q matrix.  Then the following will convert x into an
m/p*n/q-by-p*q matrix where each row contains the elements of each
submatrix

   m <- nrow(x)                         # number of rows
   n <- ncol(x)                         # number of columns
   dim(x) <- c(p, m/p, q, n/q)          # reshape the array
   x <- aperm(x, c(2, 4, 1, 3))         # permute the dimensions
   dim(x) <- c(m/p*n/q, p*q)            # reshape again

Now you can easily perform any operation you like (mean, median,
max, min, etc.) on each row to get a m/p*n/q-by-1 vector.  For
instance, to compute the mean of each submatrix:

   out <- x %*% rep(1/(p*q), p*q)

Of course, for other operations, you might need a loop treating
each row separately.  Finally, convert to the m/p-by-n/q matrix.

   dim(out) <- c(m/p, n/q)

There, now you have computed the mean (assuming the example above)
of each block.

messages.body_plain:
Thanks to Charla Lambert and Bill Venables for their advices on how to fix
a parameter in a GAM.

*************************************************

>From Charla Lambert:

You can use the offset() function to fix coefficients in a GAM or GLM.
Some examples are:

  # Fix the coefficient of Age to be 0.01.
  > glm(Kyphosis ~ offset(0.01 * Age) + Start, family = binomial,
        data = kyphosis)

  # Fix the coefficient of Age to be 0.01 and the intercept to be 0.25.
  > glm(Kyphosis ~ offset(0.25 + 0.01 * Age) + Start - 1,
        family = binomial, data = kyphosis)

This function is largely undocumented before S+6 (currently in
production), so your question tends to come up a lot.  In S+6, however,
its help file has been updated and examples have been added to the Guide
to Statistics.

*************************************************

>From Bill Venables:

Suppose the parameter is the coefficient of x3 and you want to fix it
at 6.  Then you only need to fit the model using

        glm(y ~ x1 + x2 + offset(6*x3), .....)
